body_text:
Mathematical proofs employ several foundational strategic
architectures:
1. *Direct Proof*: To establish $P \implies Q$, assume $P$ as a
temporary hypothesis and deduce $Q$ via inference rules. The
Deduction Theorem guarantees that this syntactic deduction
yields a proof of the implication $P \implies Q$.
2. *Proof by Contraposition*: To establish $P \implies Q$,
assume $\neg Q$ and derive $\neg P$. This strategy relies upon
the classical equivalence $(P \implies Q) \iff (\neg Q \implies
\neg P)$ and is particularly effective when the negation of $Q$
provides more constructive information than $P$.
3. *Proof by Contradiction (Reductio ad Absurdum)*: To establish
$P$, assume $\neg P$ and derive a logical contradiction
($Q \land \neg Q$). In classical logic, this guarantees the truth
of $P$ through the law of excluded middle.
